controls.name: General controls over technology
controls.description: The organization works out which of its business processes depend on technology to run correctly - which system performs the step, which one holds the record, which one moves the data between them - and then puts general controls underneath that technology rather than only around the process on top of it. Three areas are covered and named rather than left implied: the infrastructure the processes run on, so it is operated, patched, backed up and monitored to a stated standard; the security administration of that infrastructure, so administrative access is granted, reviewed and removed deliberately and privileged action is traceable to a person; and the acquisition, development and maintenance of the technology itself, so anything bought, built or changed follows a defined path before it reaches production. The dependency map and the controls answering it are revisited when a process is redesigned or a system replaced, so a control is not left pointed at technology the process no longer uses.

controls.name: Capacity management
controls.description: How much of each system component is actually in use - compute, memory, storage, database connections, network throughput, licences, queue depth - is measured continuously rather than inspected after a slowdown, and each measurement is held against the level at which that component stops meeting the commitments made for it. Demand is projected forward from that history and from what the business already knows is coming - a launch, a migration, a seasonal peak, a large customer - so the question being answered is when headroom runs out rather than whether it has. Thresholds are set below the failure point and alert somebody who can act on them; adding capacity is treated as a planned change with the lead time it really needs; and where capacity cannot be added quickly enough, what will be shed, throttled or queued is decided in advance rather than during the incident. Afterwards the projection is compared with what actually happened and the model corrected.

controls.name: Processing specifications & data definitions
controls.description: What the system is meant to process, and to what standard, is written down and kept current: the data it accepts and what each field means, the rules it applies, the outputs it produces, and the timing it commits to. Those definitions live in one place that both the people operating the system and the people relying on its output work from, so a disagreement about whether a result is right is settled against a stated specification rather than against two recollections. The parts customers and users need in order to use the service correctly are made available to them rather than held internally. A specification changes through the same controlled path as the system it describes, and each version is dated and retained, so it is possible to say afterwards which specification a given period’s processing was performed against.

controls.name: Controls over system inputs
controls.description: Data entering the system is checked where it arrives rather than after it has been processed. Every input route - a form, a file, an interface, a manual entry - has stated rules for what it will accept: which fields must be present, the format and range each must fall in, and the reference data a value has to match. Completeness is established rather than assumed, by agreeing a record count, a control total or a batch header back against the sender, so a file that arrives half-written is detected as short instead of processed as small. Where an input carries an instruction, the authority of the source is checked as part of intake, so the system acts only on instructions from a party entitled to give them. Anything that fails a check is rejected or held in a queue somebody owns, with the reason recorded and a route back to the sender to correct and resubmit - nothing is silently dropped, and nothing is silently defaulted to a value the sender did not provide.

controls.name: Controls over system processing
controls.description: Processing runs to the specification the system published, and the organization can show that it did. Each item is processed once and once only, in the sequence the specification requires, against the rules and reference data in force at the time; a duplicate is detected and rejected rather than reconciled out later. Completeness is proved through the run rather than at the end of it, by carrying counts and control totals from intake through each stage and agreeing them at the boundaries, so an item lost between two steps surfaces at the step that lost it instead of at the customer. Processing acts only on authorized instructions, and a change to a processing rule takes effect through the change process rather than through an edit to a running job. Whatever the run could not process is written to an exception queue with the reason, an owner and a deadline; exceptions are worked and cleared rather than allowed to age; and a restart after a failure resumes from a known point rather than reprocessing or skipping work.

controls.name: Controls over output and delivery
controls.description: Output reaches the people entitled to it, in the form and on the timetable the specification states, and the organization can show that what arrived is what was produced. Recipients and delivery routes are defined in advance rather than added ad hoc, and output carrying confidential or personal data is protected in transit and released only to the recipient it was prepared for. Delivery is confirmed rather than assumed - by acknowledgement, by a transmission log, or by agreeing a record count or total with the recipient - and a failed or partial delivery raises an alert to somebody who resends it, instead of being discovered by the recipient. Output that is late against the committed timetable is recorded as late and the recipient is told. Distribution lists are reviewed on a stated cadence, so output does not keep flowing to somebody who is no longer entitled to receive it.

controls.name: Storage of inputs, work in progress and outputs
controls.description: Data is stored completely and accurately at every stage it passes through - as received, while it is part-processed, and once it is finished - so a run can be reconstructed afterwards rather than only its result inspected. Where each stage is held, for how long, and who may reach it are decided in advance and kept consistent with the retention policy rather than with whatever the storage tier happens to do. Stored data is protected against loss and against undetected alteration: it is backed up, and it is checked back against the stage before it by count, total, checksum or reconciliation, with a failed check raising an alert to somebody who investigates it. Retrieval is exercised rather than assumed - data is confirmed to come back intact, in a usable form, inside the time the service commits to - and an item that cannot be retrieved or will not reconcile is treated as an exception with an owner rather than as an anomaly.

controls.name: Choice & consent for personal information
controls.description: Before personal information is collected, the person it is about is told what choices they have over it - what they may decline, what they can turn off later, and what declining will mean for the service they receive - in words that state the consequence rather than implying it. The choice is captured as a positive act and recorded together with what was presented, when, and by which route, so the organization can show later what a person actually agreed to rather than what today’s form says. Where the information is of a kind that needs explicit agreement, that agreement is asked for separately and obtained before the collection happens, not bundled into a general acceptance of terms. Where agreement is sought inside a written declaration that also covers other matters - terms of service, an employment contract, an order form - the request for it is presented so that it clearly stands out from the rest, in a form that is intelligible and easy to get at, in clear and plain language, rather than reading as one clause among many. Agreement is asked for only where the person is genuinely free to refuse: the organization does not make a service or a contract conditional on agreeing to processing that the service or contract does not actually need, and where it depends on agreement it can say what it is needed for. Before the person agrees, they are told that they may take the agreement back at any time and that doing so does not make what was already done unlawful. A person can change or withdraw a choice by a route no harder than the one that gave it; the change takes effect in the systems that act on it rather than only in the record of it; and the record is added to rather than overwritten, so the history of what was agreed survives.

controls.name: Collection limited to disclosed purposes
controls.description: What personal information is collected is decided against the purposes the organization has disclosed, and every field collected is tied to one of them; a field nobody can tie to a purpose is not collected. All the routes information actually arrives by are inventoried - forms, interfaces, imports, third-party sources, and the data generated as a by-product of somebody using the service - so what is gathered is known rather than inferred from the form design. Collection is by lawful and fair means: the person knows it is happening, and a route that works only because they do not notice it is not used. Where information comes from a third party, the organization establishes what that party was actually permitted to pass on before relying on it. The inventory is revisited when a purpose changes or a feature is added, and when a purpose ends the collection that served it stops.

controls.name: Use limited to disclosed purposes
controls.description: Personal information is used only for the purposes that were disclosed and agreed to, and the limit is enforced where the use happens rather than stated only in a policy: datasets and systems carry the purpose the data was collected for, and a new use is checked against it before it begins. A use outside those purposes - a new analysis, a new feature, a new audience, training a model, a secondary use by another team - is treated as a change that requires either a fresh disclosure and a fresh choice, or a recorded decision that it is compatible with the original purpose together with the reasoning for that. Where the new purpose rests on neither a fresh consent nor a law that provides for it, the compatibility decision is made against stated factors rather than asserted: any link between the purpose the data was collected for and the intended new one; the context in which it was collected, and in particular what the people concerned would reasonably expect given their relationship with the organization; the nature of the data, and whether it includes the categories that carry extra protection or data about criminal convictions and offences; the possible consequences of the intended use for those people; and the safeguards that would apply to it, which may include encryption or pseudonymization. Copies and extracts inherit the limits of the source, so a purpose is not lost when data moves into a warehouse, a test environment or a spreadsheet, and an internal request for personal data is answered against the purpose it was collected for rather than against the seniority of whoever asked.

controls.name: Authorized disclosure of personal information
controls.description: Personal information leaves the organization only for a purpose it has disclosed and on the consent or other authority it obtained, and that is checked before the disclosure rather than reconstructed after it. Standing disclosures - a processor, a partner, an integration a customer has switched on - are approved in advance, listed, and tied to the purpose and the authority that permits them, and the list is reviewed rather than left to accumulate. A one-off request, including one from a law-enforcement or government body, goes to a named role who establishes what is being asked for, on what authority, and how much of it is genuinely required, and who releases the minimum that answers it; where the organization is permitted to tell the person concerned, it does. A demand that arrives as a judgment of a court or a decision of an administrative authority in another country is not treated as compelling disclosure on its face: it is recognized or enforced only where it rests on an international agreement in force - a mutual legal assistance treaty or equivalent - between that country and the jurisdiction the organization answers to, and where it does not, the organization looks for a separate lawful ground for the transfer instead of complying because a document looked official, takes advice before responding, and records what it decided and why. Everyone who can release personal information knows this is the only route, and a release outside it is handled as an incident rather than as an exception to be tidied up.

controls.name: Record of disclosures of personal information
controls.description: Every disclosure of personal information to a party outside the organization is recorded as it is made - the date, who received it, what was disclosed, the purpose, and the authority relied on - so the record is built while disclosures happen rather than reconstructed from memory once somebody asks. Disclosures that were not authorized are recorded in the same place, whether the organization detected one itself or was told of one by a recipient, a customer or a regulator, together with what went out, how it happened, and what was done about it - so an unauthorized disclosure is not invisible for having been unintended, and the two kinds can be answered together. On request, an individual is told what personal information the organization holds about them and who it has been disclosed to, drawn from that record and provided inside the time the organization has committed to; where a category of disclosure is left out of what is reported, that exclusion is stated in advance rather than decided request by request. The same record is what makes a downstream correction possible: where personal information is corrected, erased, or its processing restricted, that change is communicated to each recipient the information was disclosed to, so the parties acting on it are working from the corrected position rather than from what they were originally sent. Where communicating it would genuinely be impossible or take disproportionate effort, that conclusion is recorded against the entry with its reason rather than reached silently, and the individual is told which recipients received their information whenever they ask.

controls.name: Quality of personal information
controls.description: Personal information is kept accurate, complete and current enough for the purposes it is actually used for, and how accurate that has to be is decided per purpose rather than in general - information used to make a decision about a person carries a higher bar than information used to address an envelope. Sources are chosen and checked against that bar rather than trusted for being upstream, and information that arrived from a third party or was produced by an inference is marked as such, so a reader knows what they are relying on. Information that goes stale is refreshed or retired on a stated cadence rather than left to be assumed current, and information found to be wrong is corrected at the source as well as in the copies taken from it - and where the organization knows it has already been relied on elsewhere, the correction is passed on. Corrections and quality failures are recorded, so a source that keeps producing bad data is fixed rather than repeatedly patched.

controls.name: ESG reporting & disclosure
controls.description: An accurate summary of ESG performance is maintained or published for stakeholders.

controls.name: Environmental aspects & impacts register
controls.description: The environmental effects of the organization’s activities are identified and kept in a register - emissions to air, discharges to water and land, hazardous materials handled, and effects on habitats or land use - each with what is being done to avoid, reduce or restore it.

controls.name: Climate risk & adaptation assessment
controls.description: A periodic assessment of how physical climate hazards and transition effects could disrupt sites, supply, demand or costs, with the response for each significant exposure and an owner.

controls.name: Product & service life-cycle stewardship
controls.description: Environmental impact is considered across design, materials, packaging, use and end of life for what the organization sells, and customers are given the information they need to use, maintain and dispose of it with less impact.

controls.name: Environmental obligations register
controls.description: A current list of the environmental permits, licences, legal requirements and customer commitments that apply to the organization, each with a named owner, a renewal or reporting date, and evidence of the last check.

controls.name: Employee wellbeing & feedback
controls.description: Workers have a routine way to give feedback and raise concerns about their working experience, and the organization acts on what it hears - supporting wellbeing and development, and recording what changed.

controls.name: Human rights commitment & due diligence
controls.description: A stated commitment to respect internationally recognized human rights, backed by a periodic review of where the organization could cause, contribute to, or be linked to harm - through its own operations, its workers, its supply chain, or partners it benefits from - with particular attention to groups more exposed to that harm.

controls.name: Grievance & complaint handling
controls.description: Anyone affected by the organization - a worker, a customer, a neighbour - has a reachable route to raise a concern or a complaint, including a complaint about how their personal data is handled; every complaint received is recorded together with what was decided and done about it; cases are resolved without undue cost or delay; and outcomes are tracked so recurring causes get fixed. The route is published where the people who might need it will actually see it, and it is reachable by somebody outside the organization who has no account, no contract and no internal contact.

controls.name: Responsible marketing & substantiated claims
controls.description: Marketing, pricing and contract terms are presented truthfully, and every environmental or social claim is backed by evidence held before the claim is published.

controls.name: Product & service safety
controls.description: The safety of what the organization sells is assessed before it reaches customers, residual risks are communicated in the instructions and warnings that ship with it, and safety reports and defects are investigated and acted on.

controls.name: Accessible & inclusive service
controls.description: Products, services and support channels are checked for use by people with disabilities and by customers the market underserves, with the barriers found recorded and a plan to remove them.

controls.name: Stakeholder identification & engagement
controls.description: The people and groups affected by the organization’s decisions are identified - including the communities around its operations - engaged before decisions that change that impact, and the organization records what it changed as a result.

controls.name: Local employment, skills & community investment
controls.description: Hiring, training and giving are directed toward the communities the organization operates in - local recruitment, apprenticeships or placements where practical, and donations, volunteering or in-kind support aimed at needs the community itself has identified - with what was done recorded.

controls.name: Responsible purchasing practice
controls.description: Significant purchasing decisions consider local and smaller suppliers alongside price, and suppliers are paid on the terms agreed - with payment performance monitored, not assumed.

controls.name: Responsible political involvement
controls.description: Rules govern lobbying, political contributions and the positions taken through trade associations; what is spent and where is recorded and disclosed where required, and none of it is used to obtain improper influence.

controls.name: Fair competition
controls.description: Price fixing, bid rigging, market allocation and abuse of a dominant position are prohibited, and the staff who deal with competitors, trade associations or tenders are trained on the line they must not cross.

controls.name: Respect for property & intellectual property rights
controls.description: The organization uses others’ physical, intellectual and traditional property only with the rights to do so - licenses held and tracked for the software, content and brands it uses, and fair payment where use is agreed. That commitment is carried out through a procedure rather than an intention. A record is kept of what the organization is entitled to use and on what terms, and what is actually installed and in use is compared against that entitlement periodically, so over-deployment is found by the organization rather than by an audit. Software, media and content are acquired only from sources the organization has established are entitled to supply them, and proof of entitlement - the license, the agreement, the receipt - is retained for as long as the use continues. The terms attached to each item are observed rather than assumed generous: the permitted number of users or installations, whether it may be copied, modified, embedded in something the organization sells, or used in a commercial setting at all. Open-source components carry obligations too, and the ones attached to each - attribution, notice, source availability, reciprocal licensing of derived work - are identified before the component is adopted and met in what ships. Entitlement is disposed of or transferred deliberately when equipment or a service is retired, and people are told what the rules are so infringement is not casual. Peer-to-peer file sharing on the organization’s systems is a case of its own: it is controlled and its use documented, so the capability cannot become a route for distributing, displaying, performing or reproducing copyrighted work the organization has no right to.

controls.name: AI system inventory
controls.description: A maintained inventory of the AI systems the organization develops, deploys, or uses, with each system's purpose, owner, and risk classification.

controls.name: AI system impact assessment
controls.description: A process to assess the potential impacts of AI systems on individuals, groups, and society, and to document and act on the results. The assessment weighs both sides of the ledger. The benefits expected from the system’s intended functionality and performance are examined and written down, rather than assumed from the fact that somebody wanted to build it. So are the potential costs that follow from an expected or realized error, or from functionality and trustworthiness falling short - including the costs that are not monetary, such as time taken from the people it is used on, harm to those wrongly classified, and the erosion of trust that is expensive to rebuild - and both are read against the organization’s stated risk tolerance rather than against nothing. The team that designs, develops, deploys, evaluates or uses the technology is the team that documents its risks and potential impacts, and it does not stop at documenting them: what it found is communicated more broadly, to the people who take the deployment decision and to those who will live with it. The process is defined before it is used and then run to plan: when an impact assessment is required, who performs it, and against what criteria are settled in advance; it is performed at planned intervals and again when circumstances change; and the results of each are retained as documented information. Impacts on wider society are assessed in their own right alongside impacts on individuals and groups - effects on the environment the system operates in, on economies and livelihoods, on public discourse, and on the institutions people rely on - because a system can leave every individual user unharmed and still move something at that scale.

controls.name: Human oversight of AI
controls.description: Appropriate human oversight of AI systems, so people can understand, monitor, and intervene in how an AI system operates - the named people who hold that oversight have the competence, the authority and the access to the system to exercise it, and the system is operated in the way the instructions supplied with it specify, inside the purpose it was assessed and approved for rather than whatever use it turns out to support. Policy defines and differentiates the roles in each human-AI configuration instead of letting "a human is involved" stand for all of them: where a person decides and the system only advises, where the system decides and a person reviews before the outcome takes effect, and where the system acts alone with a person monitoring after the fact - each configuration naming who holds the oversight role, what they are expected to check, and what they are empowered to do about it. The oversight process for a given system is then defined in line with those policies, assessed against whether it actually works in practice rather than on paper, and documented.

controls.name: AI policy
controls.description: A documented, leadership-approved policy for the responsible development and use of AI, aligned with the organization’s other policies and reviewed at planned intervals. The policy is where the AI risk management process is established, rather than the process being whatever practice has grown up: it states how AI risk is assessed, who decides what, which of the organization’s risk priorities make an activity mandatory and which leave it to judgement, and what has to be recorded when a decision is taken. It is written to be read by the people it binds and published to them, so the process and the outcomes it produces rest on transparent policy, procedure and control rather than on the standing of whoever happens to be running it. Top management establishes the policy itself rather than ratifying one drafted beneath it: the policy is appropriate to the organization’s purpose, it provides the frame within which AI objectives are set, and it carries a commitment to meet the requirements that apply and to keep improving the management system. It is kept as documented information, communicated inside the organization, and made available to interested parties where that is appropriate. The policy states boundaries as well as principles - where AI may be used, where it may not, and which uses the organization has decided to prohibit outright - written as a rule somebody can be held to rather than as an aspiration, so that a proposed use can be tested against it before any work starts.

controls.name: AI roles & accountability
controls.description: Defined and allocated responsibilities for AI across the organization, plus a way for staff to raise concerns about the organization’s AI. Executive leadership holds the decisions about AI risk rather than delegating them out of sight: the decision to develop or deploy an AI system, and the acceptance of the risk that comes with it, is taken by a named executive who answers for it, and the name is recorded with the decision rather than reconstructed afterwards. One owner is named for AI governance as a whole - a single accountable role rather than a committee that shares the answer - and the responsibilities of the teams that build, buy, operate and rely on AI are defined against that ownership, so nothing lands in the gap between two functions.

controls.name: AI risk management process
controls.description: A process to identify, analyze, prioritize, and treat the risks an AI system can pose, tracked over its lifecycle. The organization’s risk tolerances for AI are determined and written down first, and the level of risk management activity a given system attracts is set against them, so a low-stakes internal tool and a system that decides something about a person are not put through the same process by default. Tracking is continuous rather than a single pass: existing, unanticipated and emergent risks are identified regularly by named people working from documented approaches, and are read against both how the system was expected to perform and how it actually performs in the context it was deployed into. Where a risk cannot be assessed with the measurement techniques available, or no metric for it exists yet, that is not treated as an absence - a tracking approach is chosen for it deliberately and recorded, so the risk stays visible while it is unmeasurable. The resources needed to manage AI risk are accounted for as part of the treatment decision, and a viable non-AI alternative system, approach or method is weighed on the same terms as any other mitigation, because not building the system is sometimes what reduces the magnitude or likelihood of the impact most. The process itself is monitored and periodically reviewed on a plan: who reviews it and how often is decided in advance and written down, and both the process and the outcomes it produced are examined, so a process that has quietly stopped surfacing anything is noticed rather than trusted. The assessment is a defined process rather than an exercise: the criteria for accepting AI risk, and the criteria for deciding when an assessment is performed at all, are set in advance and applied the same way each time, so repeated assessments produce consistent and comparable results rather than a different answer depending on who ran them. It is performed at planned intervals and again when a significant change is proposed or has happened - a new intended use, a new model, a new data source, a new population it is used on - and the results of each run are retained as documented information.

controls.name: Data governance for AI
controls.description: Governance of the data used to develop and operate AI systems: sourcing, quality, provenance, and preparation of training and operational data. Where each training and tuning dataset came from is recorded, and the organization confirms it is permitted to use it for that purpose before the data is used rather than after somebody raises the question. Data is checked for whether it is accurate and appropriate for the people and the cases the system will actually affect - representative of that population rather than of whoever was easiest to collect from - and a shortfall found is recorded and acted on instead of noted. Only the data the AI purpose needs is used: a field nobody can tie to the purpose does not enter the pipeline, and what is used is kept no longer than the purpose justifies, with the retention period stated per dataset and enforced when it ends.

controls.name: Responsible AI development lifecycle
controls.description: Objectives and processes for responsible design and development of AI systems, including requirements, design documentation, and controlled deployment. Requirements are elicited from the relevant AI actors rather than assumed by the build team - the people who will operate the system, the people it will be used on, the domain experts, and the functions accountable for it - and they are written so those people can confirm they understood them. "The system shall respect the privacy of its users" is a requirement rather than a sentiment only when it is stated as something a test could fail. Design decisions record the socio-technical implications they carry: what a choice does to the people and the process around the system, not only to its measured performance.

controls.name: AI verification, validation & robustness
controls.description: Testing that an AI system meets its requirements and performs with appropriate accuracy, robustness, and security before and during use. Safety is evaluated on its own terms and on a regular cadence, against the safety risks identified when the system was mapped: the system is demonstrated to be safe before it is deployed, its residual negative risk is shown to sit inside the stated risk tolerance rather than merely to have been reduced by some amount, and it is shown to fail safely - particularly when it is driven beyond the limits of what it knows. The safety metrics used reach reliability and robustness, what is watched in real time, and how quickly a failure of the system is responded to. Validation before go-live is a gate rather than a report: what the system has to demonstrate about meeting its intended purpose and the risk criteria set for it is decided in advance, and a system that does not meet them does not go into service. Performance is tested for stability as well as for accuracy - across the range of inputs, populations and operating conditions the system will actually meet in production, not only on the data it was built on.

controls.name: AI technical documentation
controls.description: Maintained technical documentation of an AI system’s design, development, and impact assessments, sufficient to demonstrate how it works and was built. It states the system’s knowledge limits - what it was built to handle, what it was not, and the conditions under which its output should not be relied on - together with how that output may be used and how a person oversees it, in enough detail that someone deciding whether to act on an output can decide well rather than guess. It also identifies, component by component, the internal risk controls the organization relies on for that component, third-party AI technologies and pre-trained models included, so the controls standing behind a system are documented in one place instead of being inferred from whichever team implemented each part. The documentation is written for the teams that rely on the system as much as for an assessor: its purpose, the data behind it, its limits and the use it is intended for are stated in one place they can find, and are kept current as the system changes rather than fixed at the version that was first written.

controls.name: AI system logging & record-keeping
controls.description: Automatic recording of events over an AI system’s lifetime, retained to support traceability, monitoring, and post-incident review.

controls.name: AI transparency & disclosure
controls.description: Clear information for users and interested parties, including disclosing when people are interacting with an AI system and how to use it appropriately. The risks to transparency and accountability that mapping identified are examined and documented in their own right - a decision the system contributed to that could not be explained afterwards, an outcome whose ownership would be unclear if it were challenged, a disclosure that is technically present but not usable by the person it is for - rather than being treated as discharged by the fact that a disclosure exists. The model is explained, the explanation is validated rather than asserted, and both are documented; the system’s output is interpreted within the context it is used in, so that what an output means, and what it does not mean, informs responsible use and the governance decisions taken on top of it. Negative residual risk - what is left unmitigated after treatment - is written down and passed to the people who will actually carry it: downstream acquirers who will build on the system, and end users who will act on what it produces. People are told when they are interacting with an AI system, and when AI materially shapes a decision about them, at the point it happens rather than in a policy they would have to go looking for. The basis of a consequential AI-assisted decision can be given to the person it was about in plain terms - what mattered, and what would have had to be different - rather than only as a technical account that satisfies an engineer. Information owed to parties outside the organization is provided rather than waited for: what external interested parties need to know about the organization’s AI systems - regulators, customers, the people a system is used on, and those who represent them - is determined, and there is a route by which they receive it and can come back with a question.

controls.name: AI monitoring & malfunction reporting
controls.description: Ongoing monitoring of AI systems in operation, with a process to detect, communicate, and report malfunctions and serious incidents. The process covers the risk nobody anticipated as well as the failure modes that were designed for: when a previously unknown risk is identified, there are procedures to follow rather than a meeting to convene - contain it, decide whether the system keeps running while it is understood, recover the service and the people it affected, and feed what was learned back into the risk record - and those procedures are actually followed and the run of them recorded. Monitoring is aimed at what degrades quietly as well as at what breaks: drift in the data or in the population, degradation in accuracy, and outcomes nobody expected are watched against a baseline recorded at deployment, on a stated cadence, with a threshold that triggers action rather than a chart somebody may look at. Incidents and harms are detected, recorded and responded to on a defined route with named responders, and what was learned goes back into the risk record and into the program rather than closing with the ticket.

controls.name: Responsible use of AI
controls.description: Processes and objectives for using AI systems responsibly and within their intended purpose, so deployment stays inside approved boundaries. The value a deployed system was approved for is sustained rather than assumed to persist: mechanisms are in place and actually applied to keep it doing the job as its data, its users and its context drift - scheduled review of whether it still earns its place, retraining or tuning where performance has moved, upkeep of the documentation and the instructions that travel with it, and a recorded decision when the honest answer is that it no longer does.

controls.name: AI supplier & third-party management
controls.description: Allocation of responsibilities with, and oversight of, the suppliers and third parties involved in developing or providing AI systems and components. The technology and legal risks a third-party component carries are mapped before it is adopted and re-checked while it is in use: what the component actually does, what data it was built on, what the license does and does not permit for the organization’s use of it, and whether that use risks infringing a third party’s intellectual property or other rights - with the approach for doing this in place, followed, and the result documented rather than settled in a procurement thread. Pre-trained models taken from outside and built into a system are monitored on the same terms as the parts the organization wrote, as part of regular monitoring and maintenance, because a model nobody here retrains still changes underneath the system when the provider ships a new version, deprecates the old one, or alters the terms it is offered under. And where a third-party dataset or AI system is judged high-risk, a contingency process is written and kept ready for its failure or its compromise - what the organization falls back to, who is authorized to invoke it, how service is carried on or withdrawn, and what the people relying on the system are told - so a dependency the organization does not control has a planned response instead of an improvised one. Diligence comes before the dependency: the governance, security and risk posture of a supplier whose AI the organization will rely on is assessed and the result recorded before the relationship starts, and re-checked while it runs. What the organization requires of third-party AI is then written into the contract rather than left to expectation - what the supplier may do with data it is given, what it must disclose about the model and its limits, what it must tell the organization when something changes or goes wrong, and who answers for an outcome.

controls.name: AI use case definition & context
controls.description: Before an AI system is built or bought, what it is for is written down and agreed rather than carried in the heads of the people building it. The record states the intended purpose and the uses that would be beneficial; the specific task the system will support and the method chosen to implement it - a classifier, a generative model, a recommender - so the technique is a decision that can be questioned rather than an accident of who was available; the context-specific laws, norms and expectations that apply where it will run; and the settings it is prospectively deployed into, with the types of user it will meet and what those users will expect of it. It records the organization’s mission and the goals the technology is meant to serve, and the business value or business context the system is being adopted for - and where the system already exists and is being assessed rather than proposed, that value is re-evaluated rather than inherited from whoever justified it originally. From the system’s capability, that established context and the way the system has been categorized, the targeted application scope is specified and written down: what the system is approved to be used for, and by extension what falls outside it. Assumptions and their limitations are recorded alongside, so a later reader can see what the scope rested on and notice when the ground has moved.

controls.name: AI competence & training
controls.description: The people and the partners who work with the organization’s AI are trained in AI risk management, pitched at what their duties actually are, so they can carry those duties out consistently with the policies, procedures and agreements that bind them - the people who build, the people who approve, the people who operate, the people who answer for it, and the suppliers and contractors doing any of those on the organization’s behalf. Separately from that awareness, the proficiency of the operators and practitioners who work with a system day to day is treated as a defined process rather than an assumption: what a person must be able to do with this system, including how to read its performance and its trustworthiness characteristics, is set out; they are assessed against it before they are relied on and again periodically; and the assessment is documented. Where relevant technical standards or certifications exist for the work, they are identified and the organization’s position on holding them is recorded rather than left open. Training and proficiency are refreshed when the systems change, when the risks change, or when an assessment showed somebody could not do something the role requires. The human resources the organization’s AI work needs are documented as a resource in their own right: which roles are required, what competencies each must hold, and where the gap sits between that and the people actually available - so a shortfall in people is visible on the same page as a shortfall in compute. The people who operate an AI system or act on its output are trained specifically in what it can and cannot do: the conditions under which its output should not be relied on, the failure modes it is known to have, and the correct way to use it - so its limits are known by the person taking the decision and not only by the team that built it.

controls.name: Interdisciplinary & diverse input to AI decisions
controls.description: Decisions about how AI risk is mapped, measured and managed are taken by a group assembled for the purpose rather than by whoever happened to build the system. Across the lifecycle, the people informing those decisions span disciplines - engineering, the domain the system operates in, legal, privacy, security, human factors, and the function that will actually run it - and span demographics, experience and background, because a risk that only shows up for a group nobody in the room belongs to is the risk that gets missed. Establishing the context for a system draws on the same breadth, user-experience expertise included, and on the capacity to see the system socially as well as technically. Who took part is documented, not only what was decided, so participation can be shown rather than asserted. And the opportunity to collaborate across disciplines is created deliberately - a standing forum, a review that one function cannot sign alone, time allocated to it - rather than left to whoever is free that week.

controls.name: AI risk culture, testing & information sharing
controls.description: The organization’s policies and its everyday practice push toward critical thinking and a safety-first mindset in how AI is designed, developed, deployed and used, and they do it in ways somebody can point at: questions a design review has to answer before a system proceeds, an expectation that someone will argue the case against, time set aside to look for how a system could go wrong before it does, and no cost to the person who says a system is not ready. Practice also has to make the work possible. Testing an AI system - including adversarial and red-team testing against the organization’s own systems - is permitted, resourced and expected rather than merely tolerated. There is a route by which anyone inside the organization, and anyone outside it, can identify and report an AI incident and have it picked up by someone who can act. And what is learned from that testing and from those incidents is shared: internally with the teams who need it, and externally where sharing would help others avoid the same failure and disclosure is appropriate.

controls.name: External feedback on AI impacts
controls.description: There is a stated route by which people outside the team that developed or deployed a system - its users, the communities it affects, and those who represent them - can tell the organization about the individual and societal impacts its AI is having, and a policy that says what happens next: the feedback is collected, considered, prioritized against everything else in front of the team, and integrated, rather than acknowledged and filed. End users and impacted communities can report a problem with a system and appeal an outcome it produced, through a route published where they will actually find it, and what arrives through those channels is folded into the measures the system is evaluated against - so a pattern of complaints moves a metric and not only a queue. Feedback that has been adjudicated - accepted, rejected, or accepted in part, with the reason recorded - is fed back into system design and implementation through a standing mechanism, so it reaches the next version rather than a report nobody reads. The engagement is regular and resourced: named people are responsible for running it, and it covers positive, negative and unanticipated impacts alike, because the impacts nobody predicted are the ones this is usually the only source of.

controls.name: AI test & evaluation design (TEVV)
controls.description: How an AI system will be tested and evaluated is designed in advance and the design is written down, rather than reconstructed afterwards from whatever happened to be run. Scientific integrity and test, evaluation, verification and validation considerations are identified and documented for the system: how the experiment or trial is designed; how data is collected and selected, and whether what was selected is actually available, representative and suitable for the question being asked; what would count as evidence that the system is trustworthy; and how a construct that cannot be measured directly - fairness, usefulness, harm - is turned into something that can be, with the reasoning for that choice on the record. The test sets used, the metrics computed and the tools that produced them are documented in enough detail that another team could repeat the evaluation and get a comparable answer. Where an evaluation involves human subjects it meets the requirements that apply to that, human-subject protection included, and its participants are representative of the population the system will actually meet rather than the population that was easiest to recruit. The measurement is then examined in its own right: the appropriateness of the metrics and the effectiveness of the controls already in place are reassessed on a cadence and updated, informed by reported errors and by the impacts landing on affected communities; and the effectiveness of the TEVV metrics and processes as a whole is evaluated and documented - so a measure that has stopped distinguishing a good system from a bad one is retired rather than kept because everyone is used to it.

controls.name: Independent & expert review of AI measurement
controls.description: The people assessing an AI system are not only the people who built it. Regular assessments and updates involve internal experts who did not serve as front-line developers for that system, independent assessors from outside the team or outside the organization, or both - chosen so that at least one person in the assessment has no stake in the answer. Domain experts, end users, AI actors external to the team that developed or deployed the system, and affected communities are consulted in support of those assessments to the extent the organization’s risk tolerance calls for, and that judgement of extent is itself recorded rather than left implicit. Their input then does specific work rather than sitting in an appendix. It connects the measurement approaches to the contexts the system is actually deployed into, and those approaches are documented. It informs the measurement results on trustworthiness in deployment and across the lifecycle, so that whether the system performs consistently as intended is answered with more than the developers’ own reading of their own tests, and the results are written down. And it is one of the two sources - field data about context-relevant risks and trustworthiness characteristics being the other - from which measurable improvements or declines in performance are identified and documented over time.

controls.name: AI fairness & bias evaluation
controls.description: Fairness and bias are evaluated as a measurement of their own, against the fairness and bias risks identified when the system was mapped, and the results are documented. The evaluation names the groups it is testing for and why those groups; it states the fairness measure being used and what that measure actually claims - an equal error rate and an equal outcome rate are different claims, and choosing between them is a decision that gets recorded rather than absorbed into a tool default; and it reports results per group rather than only in aggregate, since an average is precisely where a disparity hides. It reaches past the model to the data and to the deployment: bias in what was collected and how it was labeled, bias introduced by how people use or over-rely on the output, and bias that only appears in one of the contexts the system runs in. It is repeated rather than performed once before launch, because the population, the data and the use all move. Where a disparity is found, what was decided about it - mitigated, accepted with a stated reason, or the system not deployed - is recorded with the result rather than left in the analyst’s working.

controls.name: AI system deactivation & decommissioning
controls.description: An AI system can be turned off, and the organization knows how. Mechanisms exist and are exercised to supersede a system with a replacement, to disengage it from the decisions it feeds, or to deactivate it altogether when its performance or its outcomes turn out to be inconsistent with the use it was intended and approved for - and the responsibility for invoking each of those is assigned to a named role and understood by the people who would have to act, before the day they have to. Decommissioning and phasing a system out is a documented process rather than an unplugging: what depends on the system and what becomes of those dependencies; what is done with the model, the training data and the logs; what is retained so that questions about decisions the system already made can still be answered; what users and affected people are told, and when; and what takes over the function, if anything does. The process is designed so that retiring a system does not raise risk elsewhere or cost the organization the trust it built - an abrupt withdrawal, a silent fallback nobody was told about, and a record destroyed while it was still needed are the three failures it exists to prevent. Rollback belongs to the same capability rather than to a separate hope: a previous version that is known to work is retained and can be returned to, and the route back is exercised rather than assumed to exist.

controls.name: AI risk treatment & sign-off
controls.description: Every AI risk the assessment surfaced leaves it with a decision attached: mitigate it, avoid it by not building or not deploying, share or transfer it, or accept it as it stands - and the decision names the treatment, the control that delivers it, the person who owns that work, and the date it is due. The treatment is chosen against the criteria the organization set in advance for what it will accept, rather than against what is convenient to implement, and where a treatment leaves risk behind, that residual risk is written down and accepted in writing by the risk owner rather than left as the remainder nobody looked at. Sign-off comes before go-live: a system whose risks have not been treated and approved does not go into service, and the approval is recorded against the version of the system it was given for, so a later change is visibly a new question rather than covered by an old answer. The plan is then carried out and its results retained - what was actually implemented, what it changed about the risk it was raised against, and what is still open - so treatment can be shown to have happened rather than to have been planned.

controls.name: AI objectives & planning
controls.description: The organization sets objectives for what its management of AI is meant to achieve, at the functions and the levels that have to deliver them, and plans the work that gets there. Each objective is consistent with the AI policy, measurable where measuring it is possible and stated so its achievement can be judged where it is not, and it takes account of the risks and impacts the organization has identified and of the requirements that apply to it. The plan behind each objective is written rather than assumed: what will be done, which resources it needs, who is responsible for it, when it is due, and how the result will be evaluated. Objectives are communicated to the people whose work delivers them, monitored while they run, updated when what the organization does with AI changes, and retained as documented information rather than restated from memory at the next review.

controls.name: AI management performance evaluation
controls.description: What the organization will monitor and measure in order to know whether its management of AI is working is decided in advance and written down: which processes and which controls, by what method, who performs the measurement and when, and who analyzes and evaluates the results and when. The methods are chosen so that repeating them produces comparable results rather than a different answer depending on who ran them and in which quarter. The results are retained as documented information, and the evaluation - what the numbers say about whether the management system is performing and whether its controls are effective, not merely what they count - reaches the people who decide what to do about it, in time for them to do it. What is measured covers the management of AI and not only the AI: how long a concern raised about a system takes to reach a decision, how many systems went live without the assessment they required, whether the objectives set are being met and by how much - so a program that is producing documents but not outcomes is visible as one.

controls.name: AI resource documentation
controls.description: What it takes to develop and operate the organization’s AI is identified and documented rather than inferred from whoever happens to be running it. The record covers the resources each AI system depends on and, for each, enough detail that somebody else could take it over: what it is, what it is used for, who provides it, and what happens if it stops being available. The tools used to build and run AI systems are documented by name and version - the frameworks and libraries, the development and experiment-tracking environments, the evaluation harnesses, and the deployment tooling - together with the purpose each serves, so a result that cannot be reproduced can be traced to the toolchain that produced it. The systems and computing resources are documented on the same terms: the compute the organization trains and serves on, where it physically or contractually sits, the storage and networking behind it, and the capacity actually available against what the workload needs. The record is kept current as tools are adopted or dropped and as capacity changes, and it is read together with the data and human resources documented elsewhere, so the full account of what an AI system requires is assembled rather than scattered across the teams that each hold a piece of it.

controls.name: AI responsibilities toward customers
controls.description: What the organization owes the customers of its AI systems is determined and then discharged, rather than settled case by case when a customer asks. The account covers what a customer must be told before they commit - what the system does and does not do, the conditions it was built for, the known limits on its output, and what the organization expects of the customer in using it safely - and what they are entitled to afterwards: support, notice of a change that alters behavior they depend on, notice of a defect or an incident that affects them, and a route to raise a problem and get an answer with somebody accountable at the end of it. Where the customer is themselves putting the system in front of other people, the information they need to meet their own obligations is provided rather than withheld as proprietary. The responsibilities are written into the terms the relationship runs on so that they bind, and they are reviewed when the system, its intended use, or the requirements that apply to it change.

controls.name: Prohibited and high-risk AI use screening
controls.description: Every intended use of AI is screened against the categories the organization has decided it will not pursue and the categories that trigger heightened obligations, before development or procurement starts and again whenever the intended use changes. The prohibited list is stated as specific practices rather than as a principle, so that a proposal can be tested against it: an AI system that uses subliminal, purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques to materially distort a person’s behavior in a way that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm; one that exploits vulnerabilities of age, disability, or a specific social or economic situation to the same effect; one that evaluates or classifies people over a period of time by their social behavior or their personal characteristics, where the resulting social score leads to detrimental treatment in a context unrelated to where the data came from, or to treatment out of proportion to the behavior; one that predicts the risk of a person committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or on assessing personality traits; one that creates or expands facial-recognition databases through untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or from CCTV footage; one that infers the emotions of a person in the workplace or in an education institution, outside medical or safety purposes; one that categorizes individuals by their biometric data in order to deduce race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life, or sexual orientation; and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, which is barred except in the narrow, separately authorized circumstances the law itself sets out. A proposal that matches one of these is stopped rather than mitigated. A proposal that matches a heightened-risk category is escalated to the people authorized to decide it. The screening result, the reasoning, and the decision are recorded either way, so a use that was allowed is as traceable as one that was refused.

controls.name: Provider obligations for high-risk AI systems
controls.description: Where the organization is the provider of a high-risk AI system - it develops one, or has one developed, and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark - the duties that attach to that role are held as a list somebody owns rather than distributed across teams until nobody is answerable. The system is made to comply with the requirements set for high-risk AI before it is placed on the market. The provider’s name or registered trade mark, and an address at which it can be contacted, are indicated on the system or, where that is not possible, on its packaging or accompanying documentation. The documentation the law requires is kept at the disposal of national competent authorities for the full retention period, and the logs the system generates automatically are kept where they are under the provider’s control. Corrective action is taken, and the necessary information given, where a system already placed on the market is found not to conform. Conformity is demonstrated to a national competent authority on a reasoned request, which means the file is assembled and current rather than assembled when asked. Accessibility requirements are met. Each duty has a named owner and a record showing it was discharged for the specific system - because the obligation attaches to the role and not to the organization’s intentions: a deployer of somebody else’s system does not carry these, and an organization that puts its own name on a bought-in system does.

controls.name: Quality management system for high-risk AI
controls.description: A provider of a high-risk AI system runs a documented quality management system that ensures the system complies with what the law requires, set out systematically as written policies, procedures and instructions rather than as practice people have absorbed. It covers the strategy for regulatory compliance, including how conformity assessment is approached and how modifications to the system are managed; the techniques and systematic actions used for design, design control and design verification, and for development, quality control and quality assurance; the examination, test and validation procedures carried out before, during and after development, and how often each is run; the technical specifications and standards applied, and, where a harmonized standard is not applied in full or does not cover a requirement, the means used instead to meet it; the systems and procedures for data management, across acquisition, collection, analysis, labeling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation and retention; the risk management system; the setting up, implementation and maintenance of post-market monitoring; the procedures for reporting a serious incident; the handling of communication with national competent authorities, notified bodies, other operators and customers; record-keeping of the relevant documentation and information; resource management, including measures related to security of supply; and an accountability framework stating what management and other staff are each responsible for across all of it. How far each part is built out is proportionate to the size of the provider’s organization - but the degree of rigor and the level of protection needed to make the system compliant are not traded away for size.

controls.name: Conformity assessment, EU declaration & CE marking
controls.description: Before a high-risk AI system is placed on the market or put into service, it goes through the conformity assessment procedure that applies to it - and which procedure that is, assessment based on internal control or assessment involving a notified body, is a determination the organization records with the reasoning behind it, because the answer turns on which category the system falls in and on whether harmonized standards or common specifications were applied in full. Where a notified body is involved, its engagement, its findings and its certificate are held with the system’s file, and the appeal route against its decisions is known before it is needed. The provider then draws up a written EU declaration of conformity for each system, keeps it at the disposal of national competent authorities for the full period required, keeps it up to date, and treats drawing it up as the point at which responsibility for compliance is assumed rather than merely recorded. The CE marking is affixed to the system - or, where that is not possible, to its packaging or accompanying documentation - visibly, legibly and indelibly, in digital form where the system is provided digitally and the marking can be reached from the interface, and followed by the identification number of the notified body where one was involved. A substantial modification to a system that has already been assessed sends it back through a new conformity assessment, whether or not the modified system is distributed further or simply stays in use with the current deployer; and where a system continues to learn after being placed on the market, which changes were pre-determined at the original assessment and written into the technical documentation is settled at the time rather than argued afterwards.

controls.name: EU database registration for high-risk AI
controls.description: Registration in the EU database is treated as a gate in front of a system going live rather than as paperwork that follows it. The provider, or its authorized representative where it has one, registers both itself and the system in the database before the system is placed on the market or put into service, in the cases the law requires it. The same act is required where a provider has concluded that a system on the high-risk list is not in fact high-risk: that conclusion and the system are registered rather than kept internal, because the assessment is precisely what is being made visible. A deployer that is a public authority, a Union institution or body, or a person acting on their behalf, registers itself, selects the system and registers its use before putting the system into service or using it. Which section of the database an entry belongs in, and the reduced set of information that applies in the law enforcement, migration, asylum and border-control areas, is determined and recorded rather than defaulted. The organization keeps its own record of what was registered, when, and by whom, and updates the entry when what it describes changes - so the public record and the organization’s own account of its systems do not drift apart.

controls.name: Marking of AI-generated and manipulated content
controls.description: Where the organization provides an AI system that generates synthetic audio, image, video or text - a general-purpose AI system included - the system is designed and developed so that its outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and are detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. The marking is a technical solution held to a standard rather than a line in the terms of service: it is effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as is technically feasible, judged against the specificities and the limits of the content type, what implementing it costs, and the generally acknowledged state of the art - and it is re-tested when the generation pipeline changes, because a marking that survived last quarter’s encoder is not evidence about this one. The organization records which of its systems this applies to and which it has determined it does not: a system performing an assistive function for standard editing, or one that does not substantially alter the input the deployer provided or the meaning of it, with the reasoning written down, so an exclusion is an argument on the page rather than a silence. Separately from the machine-readable case, content that is generated or materially altered by AI is labeled to the people who will see it wherever its nature would otherwise mislead them, in terms they will actually read, at the point they encounter it.

controls.name: Deep fake and published AI text disclosure
controls.description: Where the organization deploys an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake, it discloses that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. The disclosure reaches the person seeing the content clearly and distinguishably, at the latest at the time of first exposure, and it conforms to the accessibility requirements that apply, so it is available to people who cannot perceive it the usual way. Where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or program, the duty narrows to disclosing the existence of the generated or manipulated content in a manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work - a narrower duty rather than an exemption, and the judgment that it applies is recorded. A second case runs alongside it: text generated or manipulated by AI and published to inform the public on a matter of public interest is disclosed as such, unless a natural or legal person held editorial responsibility for the publication after a process of human review or editorial control - and where the organization relies on that, who held the responsibility and what the review consisted of is recorded rather than asserted. This is a duty of the deployer, and it is not discharged by a provider’s machine-readable marking, which serves a different audience and a different purpose.

controls.name: Notice for emotion recognition & biometric categorization
controls.description: Where the organization deploys an emotion recognition system or a biometric categorization system that it is permitted to run, the people exposed to it are informed of the system’s operation - what it does, that they are subject to it, and where to find out more - clearly and distinguishably, at the latest at the time of first exposure, and in a form that conforms to the applicable accessibility requirements. Notice reaches everyone exposed rather than only those who interact with the system deliberately, because exposure to a biometric or emotion-inference system is usually passive: a person walks into range rather than opening an app. The personal data such a system processes is handled under the data-protection law that applies to it, on a recorded lawful ground, with retention and the rights of the people concerned settled as they would be for any other processing rather than treated as incidental to the system. Where the organization relies on the narrow permission the law provides for detecting, preventing or investigating criminal offences, the basis for relying on it and the safeguards applied are recorded, because the notice duty otherwise stands. This is a deployer’s duty, and running a permitted system without telling the people in front of it is the failure it exists to prevent.

controls.name: General-purpose AI model technical documentation
controls.description: A provider of a general-purpose AI model draws up technical documentation of the model and keeps it up to date, covering the training and testing process and the results of the model’s evaluation, at least to the level of detail the Regulation’s own annex sets as the minimum. The documentation exists in order to be handed over: it is kept ready to provide, on request, to the AI Office and to national competent authorities, which means it is maintained in a form somebody outside the team can read and is not reconstructed from notebooks when the request arrives. Each material change to the model - a new training run, a new released version, a change of data or of evaluation result - updates the documentation rather than accumulating against it, and the version of the documentation is tied to the version of the model it describes, so a reader can tell which model they are reading about. Where the organization relies on the exception for a model released under a free and open-source license that allows access, use, modification and distribution, and whose parameters, architecture information and usage information are publicly available, the basis for relying on it is recorded - together with the fact that the exception does not survive the model being classified as one with systemic risk.

controls.name: Information for downstream providers of a GPAI model
controls.description: A provider of a general-purpose AI model draws up, keeps up to date, and makes available the information and documentation that providers of AI systems intending to integrate the model actually need. The test is what the downstream provider can do with it: understand the capabilities and the limitations of the model well enough to build responsibly on it, and comply with the obligations the Regulation puts on them for the system they are placing on the market - neither of which can be done from a marketing page. The content includes at least the elements the Regulation’s annex enumerates, and it is supplied in a form that travels with the integration rather than being available on request to whoever thinks to ask for it. Intellectual property rights, confidential business information and trade secrets are observed and protected while this is done, which shapes how the information is expressed but is not a reason to withhold what a downstream provider needs in order to meet its own duties. The organization keeps a record of who received which version, so that a downstream provider building on a description that has stopped being true can be told.

controls.name: AI copyright & intellectual-property compliance
controls.description: The organization checks that what goes into its AI systems, and what comes out of them, respects other people’s intellectual property and the terms the material was made available under. Inputs are checked before use: training and tuning data, models, code and content taken from outside carry licenses, and what each license actually permits for this use - commercial use, redistribution, incorporation into a product the organization sells, retention of the weights derived from it - is established and recorded rather than assumed generous. Outputs are checked as well, because a system can produce material that infringes even where every input was licensed, and what the organization will do when that happens is decided in advance rather than during the complaint. Where the organization provides a general-purpose AI model, it additionally puts in place a policy to comply with Union law on copyright and related rights, and that policy is operative rather than declaratory: it identifies reservations of rights expressed by rightsholders against text and data mining and complies with them, using state-of-the-art technology to do so, and it is revisited as the means of expressing and detecting those reservations move. Who owns the policy, what it requires of a training run before the run starts, and the record of a run having been checked against it are held rather than left with whichever team launched the job.

controls.name: Public summary of GPAI training content
controls.description: A provider of a general-purpose AI model draws up a summary of the content used to train the model and makes that summary publicly available, following the template the AI Office provides rather than a format of the organization’s own choosing. Sufficiently detailed is the standard the Regulation sets and the standard the summary is written to: detailed enough for parties with a legitimate interest, rightsholders in particular, to understand what kinds of content the model was trained on and to act on that understanding. The summary is published where it can be found from the model’s own documentation, is dated and versioned against the model release it describes, and is updated when a further training run changes the answer. Producing it is treated as a consequence of the data-provenance record the organization already keeps rather than as a separate research exercise, which is what makes keeping it current possible - a provider that cannot say internally what it trained on cannot publish an honest summary of it.

controls.name: Systemic-risk obligations for GPAI models
controls.description: Where a general-purpose AI model the organization provides is one with systemic risk, four further duties run on top of everything required of any such model. Model evaluation is performed in accordance with standardized protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, and it includes adversarial testing conducted and documented with the explicit aim of identifying and mitigating systemic risks rather than of producing a benchmark score. Possible systemic risks at Union level are assessed and mitigated, their sources included, across the model’s development, its placing on the market and its use - so a risk that arises from how others deploy the model is in scope, not only one that arises in training. Relevant information about serious incidents, and the corrective measures possible against them, is kept track of, documented, and reported without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national competent authorities - which requires a route set up in advance and known to the people who would have to use it at speed, not discovered during the incident. And an adequate level of cybersecurity protection is maintained for the model and for the physical infrastructure it runs on, weights and training pipeline included, since the harm from a model with systemic risk being taken is not the same harm as a general breach. The organization also records how it knows whether the model meets the classification at all, and notifies where the law requires it, so the answer is a position the organization holds rather than one it discovers.

controls.name: Security of AI models, data & pipelines
controls.description: The models, the data behind them and the pipelines that build and serve them are brought inside the organization’s information-security program rather than run as a research environment beside it.
